To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

decidual NK cells are the main source of chemokines that regulate trophoblastic invasion and angiogenesis in the decidua and that this occurs via specific interactions between decidual NK cell activating and inhibitory receptors and trophoblastic ligands.
decidual NK cells regulate the invasion of the semiallogenic fetal cells in the decidua and trophoblast induced angiogenesis by production of specific cytokines and angiogenic growth factors.
decidual NK cells are potent producers of chemokines and angiogenic factors that are essential for trophoblast and vascular development in the decidua.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of dNK cells in human pregnancy.

the identification of novel mechanisms of maternal-fetal tolerance at the human fetal-maternal interface and the development of novel strategies for the prevention of pre-eclampsia and recurrent miscarriage.
the identification and characterization of the mechanisms by which the immune system is involved in pregnancy and the regulation of trophoblast development and invasion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dNK cells are not 'immune suppressors' but are essential to ensure a proper development of the fetal placenta.

the human dNK cells are the key regulatory cell type at the maternal fetal interface and that they are involved in a variety of functions including regulation of trophoblast differentiation and invasion, angiogenesis and vascular remodeling and immune cell recruitment.
dNK cells are essential to support trophoblast growth, invasion and vascularization of the decidua, by a complex network of interactions between dNK cells and the maternal decidua.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dNK cells are the major players in the maternal-fetal interface and that they have a critical role in regulating the trophoblast invasive process and vascular growth in the maternal deciduas.
dNK cells are not only the main regulators of trophoblast development, but they also contribute to the establishment of a vascularized and functional placenta.
decidual NK cells are not 'passive bystanders' at the fetal maternal interfaces, rather, they actively regulate the development of the placenta and fetal vascular system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dNK cells are not only important to prevent maternal rejection of the fetus, but also to support the growth and development of the fetal tissues.
dNK cells play a key role in regulating trophoblast and vascular development at the fetal maternal interfaces.

dNK cells play a critical role in the regulation of key developmental processes at human fetal maternal interface, including trophoblast invasiveness, vascular growth and angiogenesis, by secretion of specific angiogenic factors.
